structure.overview: The case concerns Mr. Stanchfield's application for judicial review of the Minister's refusal to delete his Social Insurance Number (SIN) and related information, seeking mandamus to deregister. The Applicant argues that since he is not currently employed or intending to be employed, he should not be required to maintain a SIN under the Employment Insurance Act and DESDA. The Federal Court dismissed the application, finding the Applicant's interpretation unreasonable and that the Minister lacks the power to rescind SINs, upholding the reasonableness standard of review.

sections.label: Additional comments on standard of review

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The decision concerns the Minister's refusal to delete the Applicant's SIN and related info, with the Applicant seeking mandamus to deregister.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section 28.1(1) of DESDA requires persons employed in insurable employment or self-employed under the Employment Insurance Act to be registered with the Commission.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argues 'who is employed' means currently employed, so not employed or intending to be employed means no registration or SIN required.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Stanchfield is self-represented, experienced in litigation, and has unsuccessfully challenged the Minister of National Revenue before.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Stanchfield applied for a SIN at age 15 in 1986 but has not been employed in insurable employment or self-employed since December 31, 2009.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: In May 2016, the Applicant sought to rescind his SIN; the Register Office responded that a SIN is permanent and cannot be disassociated from the individual.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: From February 2017, communications between the Applicant and Department officials escalated, with the Applicant demanding rescission and the Department refusing.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The interactions add nothing to the issues; no unfair treatment or lack of serious consideration of the Applicant's rescission demand is suggested.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant suggested the SIN regime offends his religious beliefs, but this issue and any Charter breach were not substantively raised.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: A SIN is a nine-digit number identifying Canadians and residents who earn money, pay taxes, contribute to pensions, or use government services.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Register is a database storing all SINs issued since 1964 with personal identifying information, updated as needed.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Various government departments use SINs for program administration and benefits, with access limited to legislated purposes.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondents identified programs requiring SINs, including Canada Pension Plan, Old Age Security, Employment Insurance, and others.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Having a SIN does not legally require participation in government programs, but without one, a person is practically excluded from them.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The central issue is whether DESDA allows deregistration of a SIN and if the Court should order deregistration and deletion of the Applicant's info.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant asserts correctness as the standard of review; Respondents argue for reasonableness; the Court finds the issue largely immaterial.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: In Vavilov, the Supreme Court held reasonableness is the presumption for statutory interpretation, but single reasonable interpretations are addressed.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The FCA applied reasonableness standard even when only one reasonable interpretation existed in Nova Tube v Conares Metal Supply.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: This case is not of central importance categories in Vavilov that require correctness standard, such as parliamentary privilege or religious neutrality.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Though the issue affects the public and is of wider concern, that alone does not trigger the correctness standard under Vavilov.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondents bring experience and objectivity, supporting a reasonableness standard leading to one reasonable interpretation.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section 28.1(1) of DESDA requires persons employed in insurable employment or self-employed under the Employment Insurance Act to register with the Commission.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Sections 28.1(2) and (3) require the Commission to maintain a register and assign a SIN to each registered person.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section 28.2 outlines the contents of the Social Insurance Register, including names, SINs, and other identifying information, and issuance of SIN cards.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Sections 28.2(8)-(10) allow issuance of a new SIN only in limited circumstances, and old SINs are voided, not rescinded.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: DESDA gives the Minister broad powers and confers operational requirements and powers on the Commission.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 28.1 requires employed persons to register but is silent on any requirement to continue employment.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The legislative scheme is silent on rescission of a SIN; old SINs are voided but not deleted or rescinded when new SINs issued.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No statutory power authorizes rescission of a SIN; Parliament would have specified such a right if intended.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant's interpretation based on 'is employed' as a continuing condition is not a true ordinary meaning interpretation.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the Applicant's interpretation unreasonable as it ignores timing and consequences of registration changes in employment history.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court must consider s 12 of the Interpretation Act and modern interpretation principles from Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant's interpretation conflicts with the statutory scheme lacking provisions for rescission or deregistration, only voidability for fraud or error.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Respondents' interpretation aligns with the purpose of maintaining a single government number and administrative consistency across federal legislation.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The interpretation supports individuals' participation in benefits and efficient monetary collection for programs and entitlements.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant's argument of voluntary enfranchisement is rejected; the registration relationship is statutory and compulsory without consent.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court concludes the Respondents lack power and the Applicant lacks right to rescind the SIN; mandamus relief submissions are irrelevant.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The judicial review application is dismissed with costs of $3,500.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: A reasonableness review does not require de novo analysis but may identify a single reasonable interpretation from text, context, and purpose.
